items.prompt: A web application needs host and path routing, redirects, and HTTP-aware health checks. Which load balancer should be evaluated?
constraints: Rules differ by host and path.

options.text: Evaluate an Application Load Balancer with listener rules, target groups, TLS termination, and HTTP health checks sized for the required request patterns.
Use a Network Load Balancer because it provides host and path routing at layer 4.
Use a gateway load balancer because it is the universal web routing option.
Use Route 53 records alone because DNS can inspect HTTP paths.

feedback.Reason: ALB provides HTTP-aware listener rules and target-group behavior for application-layer routing.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ALB operates at the application layer and can route using host, path, headers, and other HTTP attributes.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect defines listener rules, TLS policy, target health, and rule priority and tests unmatched requests.
Details.errorCorrection: NLB is transport-layer, GWLB inserts appliances, and DNS cannot inspect URL paths.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: ALB simplifies application routing but adds layer-7 processing and is not a transparent arbitrary TCP proxy.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: NLB does not provide ALB-style host and path rule evaluation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: GWLB is for virtual appliances, not generic HTTP routing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS routing operates before the HTTP request path is available.

items.prompt: A TCP service requires static IP addresses, high connection rates, and client source IP preservation. Which load balancer fits best?

options.text: Evaluate a Network Load Balancer with static or elastic IP options, TCP or TLS listeners, target health, and source-address behavior validated for the service.
Use an Application Load Balancer because all TCP services can be converted to HTTP automatically.
Use a gateway load balancer because it provides static application IPs for every target.
Use a public IP on every target and distribute clients with round-robin DNS only.

feedback.Reason: NLB targets transport-layer high connection workloads and supports static address use cases.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: NLB operates at layer 4 and can provide static IPs per AZ and preserve or expose source information according to target mode.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests client allowlists, TLS termination or pass-through, health checks, and AZ behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: ALB does not convert arbitrary TCP to HTTP, GWLB is appliance insertion, and DNS round-robin lacks health and connection-state control.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: NLB offers high performance and transport flexibility but fewer application-layer routing features.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An ALB requires HTTP or HTTPS application traffic.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: GWLB uses GENEVE appliance forwarding rather than serving as a generic TCP endpoint.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS round robin lacks managed health, connection draining, and static per-AZ load-balancer behavior.

items.prompt: A security appliance fleet must inspect traffic without each application knowing the appliance addresses. Which service should be evaluated?
constraints: Traffic must pass through the fleet.

options.text: Evaluate a Gateway Load Balancer with appliance target groups and endpoint-service integration, validating GENEVE support, route insertion, health, and symmetric flows.
Use an ALB because application-layer rules automatically steer packets through appliances.
Use an NLB and assume it distributes appliance state without a service insertion path.
Place appliances behind Route 53 because DNS is a transparent packet bridge.

feedback.Reason: GWLB is purpose-built to deploy and scale virtual appliances through a transparent service insertion model.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: GWLB uses GENEVE and endpoint services to steer traffic to appliance targets while abstracting fleet instances.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect designs route tables, return paths, appliance health, and failure behavior before production.
Details.errorCorrection: ALB is HTTP-aware, NLB is not an appliance insertion abstraction, and DNS cannot bridge packets.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: GWLB simplifies appliance fleet scaling but adds encapsulation and routing complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: ALB rules do not transparently insert packet inspection appliances.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: NLB alone does not provide the GWLB appliance service model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS resolves names and does not forward arbitrary packets.

items.prompt: A web fleet needs centralized certificate management and HTTP routing, while backend connections may remain HTTP inside a private VPC. What should be configured?

options.text: Terminate TLS at an ALB using an appropriate certificate and security policy, then route to private targets while deciding whether backend encryption is also required.
Terminate TLS only on each instance and use an unconfigured TCP load balancer for host routing.
Store certificates in DNS records so the load balancer can discover them.
Disable certificate validation between client and load balancer to improve performance.

feedback.Reason: ALB can centralize HTTPS termination and HTTP-aware routing while keeping targets private.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Listeners can use ACM certificates and security policies; target groups separately define backend protocol and health behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner manages certificates, chooses backend encryption from threat and compliance requirements, and tests renewal and redirects.
Details.errorCorrection: Instance-only termination duplicates certificate work, DNS does not store certificates, and disabling validation weakens security.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Central termination simplifies operations but requires a clear trust boundary for traffic from load balancer to target.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: TCP load balancing does not provide host or path routing, and instance-only certificates add operations.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Certificates are managed through certificate services and listener configuration, not DNS records.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Certificate validation is a security requirement, not a safe performance toggle.

items.prompt: Two ALB path rules overlap and requests reach the wrong service. What should be reviewed?

options.text: Order rules from the most specific intended match to broader matches, verify priority and default action, and test representative paths and query behavior.
Add another default action because default actions are evaluated before listener rules.
Use security groups to select the ALB rule target.
Create more target groups without changing listener rule evaluation.

feedback.Reason: ALB listener rules are evaluated by priority, so overlapping patterns need deliberate ordering.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The first matching listener rule determines the action; unmatched traffic uses the default action.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner keeps rule priorities explicit and tests both matching and unmatched paths after changes.
Details.errorCorrection: The default is used only after no rule matches, security groups do not choose target groups, and target-group count does not change rules.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More rules increase routing flexibility but raise review and testing complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Default action is not evaluated before matching listener rules.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security groups govern network reachability, not application rule selection.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Target groups need a listener action or other routing reference to receive traffic.

items.prompt: An ALB sends traffic to a target that accepts TCP but returns HTTP 500 on the health URL. What should be corrected?
constraints: The application has a readiness endpoint.
The listener and target ports are known.

options.text: Configure a health check that tests the target's real readiness path, protocol, port, expected status, timeout, interval, and healthy or unhealthy thresholds.
Use a ping to the instance IP because network reachability proves application readiness.
Increase the load balancer idle timeout because a failed health response is always a client timeout.
Disable health checks so every target receives a share of traffic.

feedback.Reason: Health checks must represent the traffic-serving readiness contract, not only port reachability.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Load balancers route only to targets that pass configured health checks and thresholds.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner uses a lightweight dependency-aware readiness endpoint and avoids making health checks more fragile than requests.
Details.errorCorrection: ICMP or a port check can pass while the application is unhealthy, idle timeout is a different concern, and disabling checks routes bad targets.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Deeper checks improve signal but can fail from downstream dependency noise; readiness scope needs deliberate design.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Network reachability does not prove application readiness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Health response failure is not necessarily an idle-timeout issue.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Disabling checks sends traffic to unhealthy targets.

items.prompt: A deployment terminates targets while long requests are still running. Which setting should be tested?
constraints: New requests should stop before termination.

options.text: Use target deregistration delay or connection draining with application graceful shutdown, and set the window from measured request duration and deployment SLO.
Terminate immediately because the load balancer retries every in-flight request transparently.
Increase DNS TTL so clients keep using the terminating target.
Disable target health changes during deployment so traffic remains balanced.

feedback.Reason: Connection draining gives existing requests time to finish while removing a target from new routing.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Deregistration behavior stops new connections and waits or times out existing connections according to the target group setting.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner coordinates lifecycle hooks, request budgets, and termination behavior and observes errors during rollout.
Details.errorCorrection: Load balancers do not guarantee replay of non-idempotent in-flight requests, DNS TTL is unrelated to target draining, and disabling health changes routes bad targets.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Long drain windows protect requests but slow deployments and consume capacity during rollout.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Transparent retry cannot safely replay every in-flight request.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: DNS does not determine target-group draining for an existing load-balancer connection.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Health state must reflect lifecycle and target readiness.

items.prompt: A stateful application uses ALB session stickiness and one target becomes overloaded. What should be reviewed?

options.text: Measure stickiness distribution and session behavior, then externalize or replicate session state where possible and reduce stickiness when the application can be stateless.
Increase stickiness duration because it always improves load balance.
Add targets without checking whether sticky clients will reach them.
Use a security group rule to rebalance existing sticky sessions.

feedback.Reason: Stickiness preserves client affinity but can create uneven load and limits the effect of adding targets.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A sticky cookie or source-based affinity sends a client to the same target for a period, so distribution follows client populations rather than request count.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner moves session state to a shared store where appropriate and uses stickiness only when required.
Details.errorCorrection: Longer stickiness can worsen skew, new targets may receive fewer existing sessions, and security groups do not rebalance load-balancer state.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Stickiness can simplify legacy sessions but reduces elasticity and resilience for target-local state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Longer affinity can increase rather than reduce skew.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Sticky clients may remain on old targets and not use new capacity immediately.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security groups do not control ALB session affinity.

items.prompt: Newly launched targets receive a full share of traffic before caches and JIT warm up. Which feature should be evaluated?
constraints: The target group supports the feature.

options.text: Evaluate target slow start or an equivalent weighted rollout, and set the ramp from measured warm-up and cache behavior while monitoring errors and latency.
Disable health checks so new targets warm through failed requests.
Use a longer DNS TTL because the load balancer sends traffic by DNS cache.
Send all traffic to one new target first to warm it faster.

feedback.Reason: Slow start reduces abrupt load on newly healthy targets while they initialize application state.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A target group can gradually increase traffic to new targets for supported protocols and configurations.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner chooses the warm-up interval from tests and removes the feature if it masks a capacity or readiness defect.
Details.errorCorrection: Failed requests are not safe warm-up, DNS TTL does not select ALB targets, and concentrating traffic on one target defeats ramping.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Slower ramping protects warm-up but delays full capacity contribution.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Health checks should protect users, not use failures as warm-up.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: ALB target selection is not controlled by client DNS TTL.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Concentrating all traffic increases overload risk during warm-up.

items.prompt: Targets are unevenly distributed across AZs and one AZ receives much more traffic. What setting and tradeoff should be checked?
constraints: Targets have different counts by AZ.

options.text: Evaluate cross-zone load balancing and target distribution together, measuring utilization, cross-AZ transfer, failure behavior, and the service-specific default.
Assume disabling cross-zone always improves both cost and utilization.
Remove the underpopulated AZ because load balancers require equal target counts.
Add a DNS record per target to balance requests independently of the load balancer.

feedback.Reason: Cross-zone behavior trades even utilization against cross-AZ traffic and depends on the load balancer type and target layout.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A load balancer can distribute within or across AZs depending on configuration and service behavior; target count affects local balance.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect compares per-AZ target scaling with cross-zone routing and tests AZ loss and cost.
Details.errorCorrection: Disabling cross-zone can leave one AZ hot, equal target count is not a universal requirement, and DNS target distribution loses managed health and draining.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Cross-zone can smooth capacity but may add transfer; local routing can reduce transfer but needs balanced targets.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Cross-zone cost and utilization depend on target distribution and service type.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Removing an AZ weakens failure resilience and is not required by the load balancer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS round robin lacks target-level health, draining, and connection management.

items.prompt: A service must preserve end-to-end TLS so the target, not the load balancer, authenticates the client certificate. Which listener design fits?
constraints: The load balancer need not inspect HTTP paths.

options.text: Evaluate an NLB TLS pass-through or transport design that preserves encrypted traffic to the target, validating client certificate handling, health checks, and source behavior.
Terminate TLS at an ALB and forward plaintext while expecting the target to validate the original client certificate.
Use a gateway load balancer because it automatically terminates application TLS for every service.
Use Route 53 health checks as the TLS proxy for target connections.

feedback.Reason: TLS pass-through keeps the encrypted session and client-certificate context at the target when that is the requirement.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: NLB can forward TLS or TCP traffic at transport level; termination location determines where certificates and client authentication are evaluated.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect tests target certificate policy, health-check protocol, and load-balancer source and connection behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: After ALB termination the target does not receive the original TLS session, GWLB is not a generic TLS terminator, and DNS is not a proxy.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Pass-through preserves end-to-end control but sacrifices centralized HTTP routing and certificate operations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: TLS termination at the ALB changes the target's certificate and client-auth context.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: GWLB provides appliance insertion, not universal application TLS termination.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Route 53 health checks do not proxy client TLS sessions.

items.prompt: A low-volume HTTP endpoint is implemented as Lambda and needs managed HTTPS and path routing. Which target type should be evaluated?
constraints: The request is HTTP or HTTPS.
The function response fits integration limits.

options.text: Evaluate an ALB target group with Lambda targets, validating invocation permissions, timeout, concurrency, health behavior, and request or response limits.
Use an NLB because it can invoke any Lambda function for arbitrary protocols.
Use a gateway load balancer because Lambda is a network appliance target.
Expose the function's private runtime address directly to clients.

feedback.Reason: ALB supports Lambda targets for HTTP request routing when the integration limits and permissions fit.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ALB invokes an associated Lambda target through a target group and listener action rather than forwarding packets to an instance.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner grants invocation permission and tests concurrency, retries, timeouts, health, and error responses.
Details.errorCorrection: NLB is not a universal Lambda protocol adapter, GWLB is for appliances, and Lambda does not expose a client-routable private runtime address.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: ALB-Lambda simplifies low-volume HTTP integration but has service-specific limits and invocation cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The stated integration is an ALB Lambda target capability, not arbitrary NLB protocol invocation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Lambda is not a GWLB appliance target.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Managed function runtimes are not directly addressed as application servers.

items.prompt: A load balancer must route to containers whose IPs change as tasks scale. Which target registration model should be used?
constraints: The service discovery system can update targets.

options.text: Use IP targets with automated registration and deregistration, and validate target health, security-group paths, draining, and address reuse behavior.
Register task IPs once and never update them because the load balancer discovers replacements automatically.
Use instance targets and assume the load balancer forwards to every task on the host without port mapping.
Expose task IPs publicly so registration remains stable across scaling.

feedback.Reason: IP targets let a load balancer address replaceable task or pod endpoints when registration is automated.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Target groups can register IP addresses in supported networks; task lifecycle must synchronize target membership and ports.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner integrates service deployment with target registration and tests rapid scale, draining, and stale IP removal.
Details.errorCorrection: Static registration leaves dead targets, instance targets have different routing semantics, and public IPs are unnecessary and unsafe.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: IP targets support fine-grained container routing but add registration lifecycle and target-count management.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Target membership must follow task replacement and scaling.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Instance target mode does not automatically express every task port and lifecycle.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Public exposure is not required for VPC IP targets and increases risk.

items.prompt: A backend authorizes clients by source address and must see the original client IP. Which NLB target behavior should be checked?
constraints: Proxy protocol is supported if needed.

options.text: Validate NLB target type and source-address behavior, enabling the supported preservation or Proxy Protocol configuration and updating backend parsing and security rules.
Assume every load balancer preserves the original IP in the network packet.
Use ALB access logs as a replacement for backend source identity in a TCP service.
Put the client IP in DNS so the target can read it from the connection.

feedback.Reason: Source IP visibility depends on load-balancer type, target mode, and protocol metadata configuration.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: NLB can preserve or convey source information according to target type and Proxy Protocol settings; backend rules must match the actual behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests instance and IP targets and validates backend parser, security groups, and client allowlists.
Details.errorCorrection: Preservation is not universal, ALB logs do not alter a TCP packet, and DNS does not carry per-connection source identity.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Source preservation can limit some target modes or routing choices and needs explicit compatibility testing.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Source visibility varies by load balancer and target configuration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Logs are observability output, not connection metadata delivered to the backend.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS answers do not encode the client's transport identity for the target.

items.prompt: A browser application uses WebSockets and long polling through an ALB. What must be validated?

options.text: Validate ALB protocol support, idle timeout, target connection handling, health checks, deployment draining, and client reconnect behavior for long-lived sessions.
Use DNS round robin because long-lived connections do not need target health.
Set an infinite idle timeout because clients must never reconnect.
Terminate every connection during deployment without a reconnect or drain policy.

feedback.Reason: Long-lived connections make timeout, target lifecycle, and reconnect behavior part of the load-balancer design.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ALB maintains client and target connections subject to idle and lifecycle settings; WebSocket upgrades and long polling have application-specific behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner sets a bounded idle policy, handles reconnect and session recovery, and tests deployments with open clients.
Details.errorCorrection: DNS lacks connection draining, infinite idle sessions consume resources, and abrupt termination loses user state.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Longer idle time supports interactive sessions but consumes connection capacity and delays cleanup.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: DNS cannot manage existing connection health or draining.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Infinite idle time can exhaust connection resources and hide dead clients.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Long-lived protocols need graceful drain and reconnect behavior.

items.prompt: A multi-tenant service routes by a validated host header and needs a default rejection for unknown hosts. What should be configured?
constraints: Unknown hosts must not reach a default tenant.

options.text: Use explicit ALB host-header rules with safe priorities and a default fixed response or rejection, and validate host normalization and certificate coverage.
Use a wildcard default action that sends unknown hosts to the first tenant.
Use security groups to distinguish HTTP host headers between tenants.
Use DNS alone and assume requests with an arbitrary Host header cannot reach the load balancer.

feedback.Reason: ALB host rules can route known tenants, while the default action must fail safely for unknown names.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Listener rules inspect HTTP host headers and choose target actions in priority order; default action handles unmatched traffic.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests certificate names, host matching, unknown tenants, and authorization beyond routing.
Details.errorCorrection: A permissive default can cross tenant boundaries, security groups cannot parse HTTP headers, and clients can send arbitrary Host headers after DNS.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Layer-7 routing is convenient but must not replace tenant authorization and input validation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A permissive default can route unknown hosts to the wrong tenant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security groups operate at network layers and do not inspect Host headers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS does not constrain the Host header a client sends to an endpoint.

items.prompt: A TCP service sees millions of short connections and ephemeral port pressure at clients. What should be measured before scaling targets?
constraints: The target service is not CPU-bound.

options.text: Correlate NLB new and active flows, client source-port limits, target connection and reset rates, listener capacity, AZ distribution, and backend accept queues.
Add target instances without checking whether the client or load balancer is the constrained side.
Increase ALB stickiness because the service is TCP-based.
Set DNS TTL to zero so every connection selects a new target directly.

feedback.Reason: High connection-rate failures can arise at clients, load balancer flow capacity, or target accept queues, not only target compute.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: NLB exposes flow and target metrics, while clients and target kernels have connection and ephemeral-port limits.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect finds the constrained layer through metrics and load tests before changing topology.
Details.errorCorrection: Extra targets do not fix client port exhaustion, ALB stickiness is not an NLB TCP control, and DNS does not direct individual established flows.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Connection-level scale requires end-to-end capacity testing rather than instance count alone.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Target count helps only when target or backend capacity is constrained.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: ALB stickiness is not the relevant control for NLB TCP flows.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS influences endpoint selection, not every connection's target selection inside the load balancer.

items.prompt: A web API has rising 5xx responses but target health remains green. Which evidence should be correlated?
constraints: Some errors may originate at the target.

options.text: Correlate ALB access logs, HTTPCode metrics, target response codes, request processing time, target health, listener rules, and application traces to identify the failing stage.
Assume green health means every request path is correct and increase target count.
Replace the load balancer because any 5xx proves the listener is broken.
Disable access logs to reduce the observed error rate.

feedback.Reason: Health checks cover a configured readiness path and do not prove every route and application response is healthy.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ALB metrics and access logs distinguish load-balancer-generated errors, target responses, rule selection, and request timing.
Details.scenarioApplication: The operator identifies whether the issue is rule, capacity, target, dependency, or client behavior before changing infrastructure.
Details.errorCorrection: Green health is narrow, extra targets may not fix rule or application errors, replacement is disproportionate, and disabling logs hides evidence.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Logging costs storage and analysis but is essential for request-level diagnosis.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Health checks validate a configured endpoint, not every request path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: 5xx can originate at targets or rules and need attribution.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Disabling telemetry cannot reduce actual customer errors.

items.prompt: A SaaS provider must expose a private service to customer VPCs without peering each VPC. Which load-balancer combination should be evaluated?
constraints: The provider controls the service VPC.

options.text: Use an endpoint service backed by a Network Load Balancer, with allowed principals, acceptance policy, private DNS, target health, and consumer routes tested.
Use an internet-facing ALB and ask each customer to allow its public IP.
Use VPC peering for every customer regardless of customer count and route overlap.
Use a NAT gateway as the provider endpoint service target.

feedback.Reason: PrivateLink endpoint services use an NLB-backed provider service and interface endpoints for consumers.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The provider publishes an endpoint service and consumers create interface endpoints whose ENIs connect privately to the service.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect controls principals, acceptance, private DNS, NLB target health, and consumer security groups.
Details.errorCorrection: Public ALB exposure is not private service access, peering does not scale as a customer mesh, and NAT is not a service target.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: PrivateLink simplifies consumer isolation but adds endpoint and service cost and provider approval governance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Public access does not meet private consumer connectivity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Per-customer peering creates route and address-management complexity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: NAT gateways provide translation, not an endpoint service target.

items.prompt: A service needs hundreds of listeners and target groups and deployment automation begins failing with quota errors. What should be reviewed?
constraints: Some listeners or groups may be duplicated.

options.text: Review service quotas, consolidate redundant rules or target groups, request justified increases, and load-test connection, rule, target, and AZ limits before further growth.
Create more load balancers without considering quotas, cost, DNS, or operational ownership.
Ignore quota failures because the load balancer automatically queues configuration changes forever.
Use security groups to store unlimited tenant routing rules instead of listener configuration.

feedback.Reason: Load balancer capacity includes documented quotas and operational configuration limits that must be designed and observed.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Listeners, rules, target groups, targets, connections, and load balancers have service quotas and per-resource behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner treats quotas as capacity inputs and automates cleanup and quota monitoring for tenants.
Details.errorCorrection: More balancers add cost and management, failed changes are not an unlimited queue, and security groups do not implement application routing.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Quota increases can support growth but should follow a simplified and tested resource model.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Resource multiplication can increase cost and operational failure modes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Configuration APIs return failures that require remediation; they are not an unlimited queue.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security groups do not store host or path routing rules.

items.prompt: An internal service needs load balancing only for VPC clients and must not have an internet route. Which scheme should be used?
constraints: The service has no public ingress.

options.text: Use an internal load balancer in private subnets with appropriate route tables, security groups, private DNS, target reachability, and multi-AZ placement.
Use an internet-facing load balancer and hide its hostname from clients.
Use a public load balancer because internal clients cannot reach private addresses.
Use a NAT gateway as the internal service's load-balancing endpoint.

feedback.Reason: An internal load balancer provides managed private access without public ingress.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Internal ALB or NLB nodes receive private addresses in selected subnets and route to private targets.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner configures private DNS and verifies client subnets, security groups, health checks, and AZ failure.
Details.errorCorrection: Hiding a public name is not access control, private clients can use internal endpoints, and NAT is not a load balancer.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Internal load balancers still need endpoint, DNS, and multi-AZ capacity design.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Name secrecy does not remove public exposure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Private clients can route to internal load balancer addresses.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: NAT provides egress translation, not target health and distribution.

items.prompt: A proposal chooses an ALB, NLB, or GWLB from product names but does not state protocol, client IP, routing, TLS, target, or failure requirements. What should the review require?
constraints: The service has latency and availability SLOs.

options.text: Map protocol and layer, routing rules, source identity, TLS termination, target type, health and draining, AZ behavior, throughput, quotas, private exposure, and cost before selecting the load balancer.
Choose ALB for every service because application routing is always the most flexible option.
Choose NLB for every service because layer 4 is always faster and more available.
Choose GWLB for every service because all traffic should pass through an appliance fleet.

feedback.Reason: Load-balancer selection is a workload and topology decision, not a universal performance ranking.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ALB, NLB, and GWLB expose different protocol, routing, target, and service-insertion models with distinct limits and costs.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect chooses the smallest fitting service and tests real traffic, failover, target lifecycle, and security boundaries.
Details.errorCorrection: ALB is not arbitrary TCP, NLB lacks application routing, and GWLB is for appliances rather than every service.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The right abstraction improves performance and operations while the wrong one creates translation, routing, or capacity debt.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: ALB is not the fit for every protocol or source-IP requirement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: NLB is not universally faster or appropriate for HTTP rule needs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: GWLB adds appliance insertion and should be used only when inspection or network functions require it.
